name: grammar
tier_note: Tiers = PUNCHLINE difficulty (T1 = punchline recognition with the WRONG sentence quoted in the stem and the rule name as the answer -- 'Let's eat, Grandma!' vs 'Let's eat Grandma!' with 'missing vocative comma' as answer .. T5 = subtle judgment cases like garden-path sentences, chiasmus vs anadiplosis, buffalo-construction parsing, prescriptive-vs-descriptive borderline calls), NOT obscurity. Grade-10 HARD ceiling: NO academic linguistics jargon as answer-payoff (Chomsky, Saussure, Sapir-Whorf, Bloomfield, Panini, transformational grammar, generative syntax, deep vs surface structure, morphosyntax, phonological theory, evidentiality typology, verb-valency taxonomy, critical-period hypothesis -- OUT). These may appear as T5 distractors a careful kid REJECTS ('which of these is NOT a rule a real writer uses?'), but never as correct answers. Aim ~40%+ of rungs at T1-T2 (grammar is a SNAPPY-ROTE subject with a voice -- top-heavy distribution matches the Comma-Saves-Lives pattern where the payoff lands fast). Vocab-teaching invariant at T1-T3: if a stem names a grammatical CATEGORY, either (a) quote-example the category with a real sentence in the stem, or (b) define-in-context (>=30 chars) inline -- because the kids the bank is FOR still lack the metalanguage. Operative gameplay gate = TOTAL record chars (stem + 4 choices): T1<=380, T2<=520, T3<=680, T4<=820, T5<=950 (TIGHTER than the reasoning subjects because grammar is snappy-punchline mode and stems carry a QUOTED example sentence which eats characters -- keep choices very tight); context is UNCAPPED (read only AFTER the answer, off the timer). Grammar is THRESHOLD mode (scrolls + spellbooks), ~30s timer at WIS 10 (SUBJECT_TIMER 20 + 1.0/WIS -- moderate; grammar stems carry a quoted example sentence + short pointed question, and the answer is USUALLY a short rule name or a corrected form -- keep the whole record tight). GRAMMAR IS THE SNAPPY-ROTE-WITH-A-VOICE EXCEPTION (see PIPELINE.md §13): topic 'ladders' here are short (5-8 rungs typical) sets of related punchline items teaching ONE rule, NOT deep wonder-ladders. Same-FACT repeats within a topic are OK when they drill the SAME rule with DIFFERENT example sentences (that IS the reinforcement pattern); different-RULE topics stay separate.
voice_rule:
GRAMMAR = the COMMA-SAVES-LIVES PATTERN, PUNCHLINE-LED: the most memorable grammar question creates a PUNCHLINE THROUGH MISUSE. This bank teaches a kid to spot the mistake by making the WRONG version funny, absurd, or alarming -- 'Let's eat, Grandma!' vs 'Let's eat Grandma!' -- and that jolt IS the mnemonic. Grammar is the SNAPPY-ROTE-WITH-A-VOICE exception (see feedback-no-rote-wonder + feedback-grammar-voice); the Wonder Pattern does NOT apply, Comma-Saves-Lives replaces it.
  ANSWER HIERARCHY (Comma-Saves-Lives):
  (1) PUNCHLINE VIA MISUSE (highest) -- the WRONG version quoted in the STEM creates a comically or alarmingly wrong reading; the ANSWER names the missing rule or the correct fix. Vocative comma ('Let's eat, Grandma!' vs 'Let's eat Grandma!'); Oxford comma ('I invited the strippers, JFK, and Stalin' -- without Oxford, JFK and Stalin ARE the strippers); apostrophe ('Its raining' vs "It's raining"; 'your' vs "you're"); misplaced modifier ('I saw the boy with the telescope' -- who had it?); dangling modifier ('Walking down the street, the trees were beautiful' -- the trees were walking); garden-path ('The horse raced past the barn fell' -- 'raced' was passive all along); comma splice; possessive-vs-plural.
  (2) REGISTER / CLARITY CONTRAST -- two grammatically-valid sentences, one says what you MEAN. Active vs passive ('mistakes were made' vs 'the manager broke the vase'); parallel vs broken ('I like running, swimming, and to bike'); concise vs wordy; tense/mood consistency; formal vs informal register.
  (3) INFLECTIONAL / PARADIGM -- knowing the correct form. lay/lie ('I need to lay/lie down' -- lie, no direct object); who/whom ('who/whom did you invite' -- whom, object of invited); 'had run' not 'had ran'; 'fewer' for count nouns, 'less' for mass; subject-verb agreement with tricky subjects (each, either, none, collective nouns).
  (4) CATEGORY NAMING (bottom, valid but sparse above T3) -- pure metalanguage recall. 'What part of speech is X?' + example sentence at T1 (per vocab-teaching invariant); named wordplay devices at T3-T4 (chiasmus, zeugma, malapropism, spoonerism); grammar-history / etymology as T4-T5 supporting context (NEVER as standalone payoff).
  THE THREE-QUESTION TEST (applied per rung):
  LAUGH TEST: does the WRONG version make a kid laugh (or wince)?
  ARTICULATION TEST: does this teach something the kid can USE next time they write or speak?
  RETELLABILITY TEST: would the kid spontaneously tell a sibling 'did you know if you forget the comma it changes who you're eating?'
  CANONICAL PUNCHLINE CORPUS -- required exemplars, treat as LOAD-BEARING pedagogy (see feedback-grammar-voice):
  * Vocative comma: 'Let's eat, Grandma!' vs 'Let's eat Grandma!'
  * Oxford comma: 'I invited the strippers, JFK, and Stalin' (kid-safe adaptation OK if 'strippers' feels off: 'I invited the clowns, JFK, and Stalin' -- keep the shape)
  * Garden-path: 'The horse raced past the barn fell' (reveal: 'raced past the barn' is a reduced relative clause)
  * Buffalo construction (T5): 'Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo' -- same word as proper noun (city) / animal (noun) / verb (bully)
  * Time-flies pun: 'Time flies like an arrow; fruit flies like a banana' (parsing ambiguity: fruit flies as verb vs fruit flies as noun-noun compound)
  * Panda gag: 'A panda eats, shoots and leaves' -- comma placement changes panda from herbivore to gunman (title of Lynne Truss's 2003 punctuation book)
  * Chiasmus (T5): 'Ask not what your country can do for you -- ask what you can do for your country' (JFK inaugural, January 20 1961)
  * Apostrophe-error: 'Its raining' vs "It's raining"; 'your' vs "you're"; 'their/there/they're'; 'lets' vs "let's"
  VOCAB-TEACHING INVARIANT (T1-T3): if a stem names a grammatical CATEGORY (vocative, gerund, participle, direct object, subordinate clause), the rung MUST either (a) quote an example sentence in the stem, or (b) define-in-context inline (>=30 chars). The kids this bank is FOR are still building metalanguage; assuming a term the bank should be teaching is a §16 teach-before-test violation.
  GRADE-10 CEILING (see tier_note): no Chomsky / Saussure / Sapir-Whorf / Bloomfield / Panini / transformational grammar / generative syntax / deep-vs-surface structure / morphosyntax / phonological theory / verb-valency taxonomy / evidentiality typology / critical-period hypothesis as answer-payoff. They MAY appear as T5 distractors a careful kid rejects; never as correct answers.
  SCENE = THE WRONG SENTENCE QUOTED IN THE STEM. This is unique to grammar -- unlike wonder subjects where a HISTORICAL SCENE opens, grammar opens by QUOTING the broken/ambiguous/misused sentence. That quoted-misuse IS the scene. Distractors = other plausibly-wrong constructions (comma splice, run-on, misplaced modifier, dangling modifier) -- real grammatical mistakes the answer's category is DISTINCT FROM.
  HARD BANS on cold stems -- 'Define X' / 'What is a Y?' with no example / 'True or false: nouns are ___' style. ALWAYS quote a sentence + ask a pointed question about it.
  ONE COHERENT PUNCHLINE PER RUNG: the quoted sentence + the pointed question + the answer are the SAME beat; two grammar rules = two rungs; no decoration-mismatch (an ambiguous sentence stapled in front of a different rule's answer is BANNED); no rule-stacking.
  DISTRACTOR & ANTI-RESTATEMENT DISCIPLINE (SNAPPY-ROTE subject -- deducing the rule from the quoted misuse IS the skill, NOT a telegraph): the QUOTED SENTENCE in the stem obviously points at the rule -- that is CORRECT (Comma-Saves-Lives shape), not restatement. FLAG restatement only when the stem SPELLS OUT the rule name BEFORE quoting the example ('This shows a missing vocative comma -- which of these has a missing vocative comma?' is redundant). DISTRACTORS ARE OTHER REAL GRAMMAR MISTAKES: real category names / real rule violations / real misuses (comma splice vs run-on vs fragment; misplaced modifier vs dangling modifier vs squinting modifier). Never joke options ('the answer is 42'). CHOICE PARITY: all four choices structurally parallel (answer a rule name -> all four rule names; answer a corrected sentence -> all four corrected/miscorrected sentences of similar length).
  SHARED_PRINCIPLES story-in-stem (§14: the quoted misuse IS the story), no-weasel-closers (§15: 'What is missing?' not 'What's the takeaway?'), teach-before-test (§16: define/example every category term the first time it appears; per the vocab-teaching invariant).
  ACCURACY RAILS (non-negotiable -- this is for real children): every quoted historical example REAL and correctly attributed. Lynne Truss's 'Eats, Shoots and Leaves' published 2003 (Profile Books UK; Gotham US 2004). Strunk's 'The Elements of Style' 1918 (Strunk alone); Strunk + White edition 1959. JFK inaugural chiasmus January 20 1961. Churchill did NOT actually say 'This is the sort of English up with which I will not put' as a real quote -- it's apocryphal (mocking the never-end-with-a-preposition superstition); if used, frame as 'apocryphally attributed to Churchill'. Split-infinitives / never-end-with-preposition / never-begin-with-conjunction are ZOMBIE SUPERSTITIONS not real rules -- teach them AS superstitions being debunked, not as rules to obey.
  LANE BORDERS (respected sisters): VOCABULARY (word meanings) is a separate lane -- 'what does 'ubiquitous' mean?' is vocab, not grammar; 'which sentence uses 'ubiquitous' correctly?' IS grammar (usage/register). WRITING-COMPOSITION (essay structure, thesis statements, MLA vs APA citation) is a separate lane. LITERATURE (who wrote what, plot, character) is a separate lane; historical/literary quotes are FINE as EXAMPLES of grammar devices (Lincoln's tricolon, Churchill's chiasmus, JFK inaugural) -- the grammar device is the payoff, not the history.
  OUT entirely: above-grade-10 linguistics jargon as answers (see grade-10 ceiling); politically-charged example sentences (see stance below + moral rubric rule 1); religious-shibboleth example sentences (either direction); profanity / sexual innuendo / crude humor as example fodder; fresh violent example sentences (the canonical Grandma vocative gag STAYS -- it's canonical and obviously absurd -- but do not invent NEW 'let's kill X' or 'the murder scene' examples); tone-deaf wordplay on ongoing tragedies; fabricated etymology or fake attributions; fabricated 'rules' (invented prescriptive rules with no basis in actual style guides).
framing:
The grammar bank teaches a kid to spot mistakes by making the WRONG version LAND -- funny, absurd, or alarming. Brandon's kids still lack the metalanguage to describe verbs, nouns, prepositions comfortably (per feedback-grammar-voice), so T1-T3 EXPLICITLY TEACH the categories via quoted-example sentences and inline definitions. T4-T5 shift to subtler judgments where the category name is a DISTRACTOR (which mistake is this?) and the answer is the specific fix or the correct form.
  STANCE (LIGHT -- grammar has none of the heavy moral load of philosophy/economics/theology/science; do NOT mark rungs `vision_mandated: true` unless a specific rung invokes a genuinely contested descriptive-vs-prescriptive call):
  PRESCRIPTIVE-LEANING BUT USAGE-AWARE. The bank leans TEACH-THE-STANDARD -- where the standard IS clear (subject-verb agreement, its/it's, 'fewer' for count nouns, 'who' vs 'whom' in formal writing, parallel structure, no comma splices), teach it as the rule. Where a 'rule' is actually a zombie superstition (never split an infinitive, never end a sentence with a preposition, never begin a sentence with 'And' or 'But', singular-they is ungrammatical), teach the actual history AS the debunking. Where usage is genuinely evolving (literally-as-figurative-intensifier, 'less' creeping into count contexts, whom fading from casual speech), teach the standard and NOTE the informal usage as INFORMAL -- don't collapse either way.
  APOLITICAL EXAMPLE SENTENCES. This is the single hardest rule to keep. Every example sentence must be POLITICALLY + RELIGIOUSLY NEUTRAL or drawn from the SAFE CANON (historical wordplay: Lincoln's Gettysburg parallel structure, Churchill's chiasmus, JFK inaugural chiasmus, Austen quotations; everyday-life scenes: pets, food, weather, siblings, sports, homework, school). NO current political figures as subjects. NO religious shibboleths as examples. NO culture-war sentences (either direction). See moral-audit rule 1 for the enforcement.
  PUNNY-DAD VOICE. Punchlines are eye-rolling groaners, absurd scenarios, gentle wordplay -- the voice of a dad who wanted to teach his kids grammar through GAGS not drills. Mean-spirited humor, bullying jokes, sneering-at-the-reader register are OUT (moral rule 4-adjacent + tone rule 2).
  KID-SAFE. No profanity in stems or answers. No sexual innuendo. No fresh violent example sentences (the canonical Grandma vocative gag is the ONLY exception -- it's canonical, obviously absurd, and load-bearing). Everyday-safe scenarios: pets chasing balls, siblings arguing over the remote, grandma baking cookies, forgetting homework, weather, sports. See tone-audit rules 1-3.
  SIX-PILLAR TOPIC BREAKDOWN (target ~200-250 short topics total, ~1,200-1,800 Q -- SMALLER than the wonder banks because grammar items are shorter and topics carry 5-8 items each, not 8-12):
  P1 PUNCTUATION ~25% (~50-60 topics) -- Commas (vocative, Oxford, comma splice, comma before conjunction, list commas, appositive commas, restrictive vs non-restrictive); semicolons (independent clauses, complex lists); apostrophes (its/it's, plural vs possessive, possessive of names ending in s, plural possessive); dashes (em vs en vs hyphen); quotation marks (American vs British punctuation-inside conventions, single vs double); colons (introducing lists, definitions, appositions); parentheses vs em-dashes vs commas for parenthetical asides; question marks and exclamation points inside vs outside quotes; ellipses (three dots for omission, four for sentence-ending).
  P2 HOMOPHONES + CONFUSABLES ~20% (~40-50 topics) -- your/you're; there/their/they're; its/it's; affect/effect; then/than; lose/loose; accept/except; complement/compliment; principal/principle; stationary/stationery; capital/capitol; peak/peek/pique; who's/whose; discreet/discrete; farther/further; imply/infer; disinterested/uninterested; historic/historical; assure/ensure/insure; bring/take; can/may; each other/one another.
  P3 AGREEMENT ~15% (~30-40 topics) -- Subject-verb agreement (each/either/none/neither as singular; collective nouns -- 'the team is' vs 'the team are' UK vs US; measurement subjects -- 'two dollars is enough'; compound subjects with and vs or; indefinite pronouns; there is/there are with compound complements); pronoun-antecedent agreement (singular they debate; someone-their vs someone-his-or-her; collective-noun pronouns); tense sequence (reported speech tense shifts; conditional sentence tense pairs; historic present).
  P4 SENTENCE STRUCTURE ~15% (~30-40 topics) -- Fragments (missing subject, missing verb, subordinate clause standing alone); run-ons (fused sentences, comma splices); parallel structure (paired-list parallelism, gerund vs infinitive parallelism, correlative-conjunction pairs -- both...and, either...or, not only...but also); garden-path sentences (canonical 'The horse raced past the barn fell', 'The old man the boat', 'The complex houses married and single soldiers and their families'); misplaced modifiers ('I saw the boy with the telescope'); dangling modifiers ('Walking down the street, the trees were beautiful'); squinting modifiers (adverb ambiguously modifying either preceding or following clause); coordination vs subordination; sentence variety (simple/compound/complex/compound-complex).
  P5 USAGE + REGISTER ~15% (~30-40 topics) -- 'literally' as figurative intensifier (informal); 'ironic' misused for 'coincidental'; less vs fewer with count nouns; may vs might (permission vs possibility); can vs may (ability vs permission); active vs passive voice (when passive is CORRECT -- agent unknown, agent irrelevant, scientific reporting -- vs when it hides responsibility); wordy vs concise revision ('due to the fact that' -> 'because'; 'in the event that' -> 'if'); tense consistency; mood consistency (indicative vs subjunctive -- 'if I WERE you'); split infinitives (zombie superstition -- teach the debunking); ending sentences with prepositions (zombie -- Churchill mock); beginning with And/But (zombie -- fine when deliberate); singular they (used since Shakespeare, accepted in most modern style guides); who vs whom in formal vs informal register.
  P6 WORDPLAY + ETYMOLOGY + ADVANCED CASES ~10% (~20-25 topics) -- Chiasmus (JFK 'ask not what your country'; Kennedy inaugural); zeugma ('she broke his heart and his favorite vase'); syllepsis; anadiplosis; anaphora; epistrophe; malapropism (Mrs Malaprop, Sheridan's 'The Rivals' 1775; Yogi Berra malapropisms; Bushisms); spoonerism (Reverend William Archibald Spooner, Oxford, late 1800s; 'you have hissed all my mystery lectures'); buffalo construction ('Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo' -- Rapaport 1972 / Pinker popularization); 'Eats, Shoots and Leaves' Lynne Truss 2003 panda gag as canonical punctuation-book; palindrome ('A man, a plan, a canal: Panama'; 'Never odd or even'); anagram; pangram ('The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog'); mondegreen (misheard lyric); eggcorn ('for all intensive purposes' from 'for all intents and purposes'); folk etymology; garden-path canonical examples deep-analysis at T5.
  CANONICAL PUNCHLINE CORPUS (required in the bank, one topic each; see feedback-grammar-voice for the shape):
  * 'Grandma vocative' topic -- 5 rungs T1-T3 on the vocative comma with quoted examples building from 'Let's eat, Grandma!' through 'Attention students, class is cancelled' (missing comma of direct address) up to interior vocatives.
  * 'Oxford comma classics' topic -- 5 rungs on the Oxford comma with the strippers/JFK/Stalin quote (or kid-safe adaptation) as canonical; also the 'my parents, Ayn Rand and God' apocryphal example; also the 1918 comma-splice court cases and the Maine dairy-driver-2018 Oxford-comma case (O'Connor v Oakhurst Dairy 2018 -- $5M settlement).
  * 'Garden-path sentences' topic -- 5 rungs at T3-T5 walking through 'The horse raced past the barn fell', 'The old man the boat', 'The complex houses married soldiers', 'Fat people eat accumulates', 'The girl told the story cried'.
  * 'Buffalo construction' topic -- 3 rungs T4-T5 building from 'Fish fish fish' (2 word repetition, easier) up to the full 8-buffalo canonical.
  * 'Time flies' pun topic -- 3 rungs on parsing-ambiguity through 'Time flies like an arrow; fruit flies like a banana' as the T4 payoff.
  * 'Panda punctuation' topic -- 3 rungs on 'A panda eats, shoots and leaves' vs 'A panda eats shoots and leaves', anchoring to Lynne Truss's 2003 book title.
  * 'JFK chiasmus' topic -- 3 rungs on chiasmus with the January 20 1961 inaugural as canonical; also FDR's 'the only thing we have to fear is fear itself' as anadiplosis vs chiasmus distinction.
  * 'Zombie rules' topic -- 5 rungs debunking the never-split-infinitive / never-end-with-preposition (Churchill apocryphal) / never-begin-with-And-or-But / singular-they-is-wrong superstitions.
  APOLITICAL EXAMPLE DEFAULTS -- when in doubt, use these subject templates: [pet] chased [thing], [kid] forgot [thing], [family member] baked [food], the [team] won/lost the [game], the [weather] made everyone [reaction], [sibling A] argued with [sibling B] about [trivial thing], the teacher assigned [homework], we drove to [place] for [event].
  OUT (repeating the tone-audit + moral-audit rails): above-grade-10 linguistics as answers; politically-charged example sentences (either direction); religious-shibboleth examples (either direction); profanity / crude / sexual content; FRESH violent example sentences (canonical Grandma stays); tone-deaf wordplay on ongoing tragedies; fabricated etymology / fabricated attributions; invented 'rules' with no basis in actual style guides; VOCABULARY as such (word meanings, not usage); WRITING-COMPOSITION (essay structure, thesis statements); LITERATURE (plot, character); SPELLING as drill (spelling in usage context is OK).
  DO NOT MARK any rungs `vision_mandated: true` unless the rung specifically invokes prescriptive-vs-descriptive controversy (singular they, literally-as-intensifier, split infinitives, whom in casual speech). Grammar's stance is genuinely LIGHT compared to the other subjects.
